metadata.document: SUBMISSION TO MINISTERIAL INQUIRY INTO LAND USES ASSOCIATED WITH THE MOBILISATION OF WOODY DEBRIS (INCLUDING FORESTRY SLASH) AND SEDIMENT IN TAIRĀWHITI / GISBORNE DISTRICT AND WAIROA DISTRICT
metadata.organisation: Environmental Defence Society and Pure Advantage

cleaned_body_text: This is a joint submission on behalf of the Environmental Defence Society (EDS) and Pure Advantage to the Ministerial Inquiry into Land Uses associated with the mobilisation of woody debris (including forestry slash) and sediment in Tairāwhiti / Gisborne District and Wairoa District. We welcome this Inquiry into land use, the mobilisation of forestry slash and sediment, and forestry practices generally, on the East Coast. Although well overdue, it presents an opportunity to clearly identify the causes of adverse effects associated with forestry activities so that these can be properly and swiftly addressed. Sustainable land stewardship on the East Coast is subject to significant physical constraints. The region is predisposed to regular high intensity rainfall events and cyclonic storms and has a geologic and geomorphic risk profile characterised by soft sedimentary rocks and medium to very steep slopes. Historic land use patterns and extensive clearance of native vegetation have made the extent and severity of erosion in the region unique. The continuing proliferation of exotic afforestation, particularly Pinus radiata, makes plain that stronger direction and more nuanced regulatory controls should be provided around what trees should be planted where in order to achieve the right tree in the right place for the right purpose. The NESPF settings are inadequate to ensure that significant adverse effects from forestry activities are avoided, attributable to a raft of regulatory flaws including reliance on the Erosion Susceptibility Classification, absence of regulatory nuance in relation to harvesting systems, and weak slash management provisions. Overcoming the entrenched extractive economy requires transformational systemic change, political courage, and a shift in societal consciousness to achieve sustainable land use and landscape stewardship.
